items.title: When a cyberattack breaks the cold chain
items.summary: For years, people have associated cyberattacks with stolen data, locked computers and disrupted digital services. However, the incident that affected numerous French supermarkets during the night of 11–12 October 2026 shows that a breach can have consequences beyond the digital world. This time, the attackers did not primarily target tills, payment systems or customer databases. Their target was the connected infrastructure used to regulate food refrigeration across different stores. This incident is particularly significant because it clearly shows how a digital vulnerability can directly affect products, facilities and physical processes. Hospitals, factories, energy providers, transport companies, logistics centres and water treatment facilities all rely on connected systems to manage physical processes. In each of these environments, an insecure configuration, poorly protected remote access or an outdated device can become an entry point. Causing a significant impact on critical or sensitive infrastructure does not always require an extremely sophisticated attack. A controller exposed to the Internet, weak credentials, insufficiently protected remote access or poor segmentation between IT and OT networks can open the door to serious operational consequences.

For years, people have associated cyberattacks with stolen data, locked computers and disrupted digital services. However, the incident that affected numerous French supermarkets during the night of 11–12 October 2026 shows that a breach can have consequences beyond the digital world.

This time, the attackers did not primarily target tills, payment systems or customer databases. Their target was the connected infrastructure used to regulate food refrigeration across different stores.

This incident is particularly significant because it clearly shows how a digital vulnerability can directly affect products, facilities and physical processes.

Hospitals, factories, energy providers, transport companies, logistics centres and water treatment facilities all rely on connected systems to manage physical processes. In each of these environments, an insecure configuration, poorly protected remote access or an outdated device can become an entry point.

Causing a significant impact on critical or sensitive infrastructure does not always require an extremely sophisticated attack. A controller exposed to the Internet, weak credentials, insufficiently protected remote access or poor segmentation between IT and OT networks can open the door to serious operational consequences.

items.title: Unmasking EvilTokens: Getting to the root of device code phishing
items.summary: Following its emergence in February 2026, EvilTokens quickly became one of the most widely used phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platforms, providing cybercriminals with AI capabilities for tailoring phishing lures and analyzing compromised inboxes to identify high-value targets. This AI-powered cybercrime platform facilitated sophisticated business email compromise (BEC) campaigns that compromised more than 12,000 inboxes in over 10,000 organizations worldwide. EvilTokens enabled threat actors to abuse the device code authentication flow, steal tokens, and compromise organizational accounts at scale using an AI-driven infrastructure and automating multiple parts of the attack chain. The toolkit offered a plethora of prebuilt phishing templates and landing pages with an AI-powered assistant to aid in structuring target-specific emails. To harden networks against the device code phishing activity described above, defenders can implement the following: - Only allow device code flow where necessary. Microsoft recommends blocking device code flow wherever possible. Where necessary, configure Microsoft Entra ID’s device code flow in your Conditional Access policies.

This AI-powered cybercrime platform facilitated sophisticated business email compromise (BEC) campaigns that compromised more than 12,000 inboxes in over 10,000 organizations worldwide.

EvilTokens enabled threat actors to abuse the device code authentication flow, steal tokens, and compromise organizational accounts at scale using an AI-driven infrastructure and automating multiple parts of the attack chain. The toolkit offered a plethora of prebuilt phishing templates and landing pages with an AI-powered assistant to aid in structuring target-specific emails.

To harden networks against the device code phishing activity described above, defenders can implement the following:
- Only allow device code flow where necessary. Microsoft recommends blocking device code flow wherever possible. Where necessary, configure Microsoft Entra ID’s device code flow in your Conditional Access policies.

items.title: When LLM Gateways Go Wrong: Findings from LiteLLM
items.summary: This security assessment of LiteLLM revealed multiple high-risk vulnerabilities that could be chained together to achieve remote code execution, arbitrary file access, and complete system compromise. The most severe issue, the missing authorization checks in /config/update combined with environment variable injection, demonstrates how a single oversight in access control can cascade into multiple high-impact exploitation paths. LiteLLM represents an important innovation in the LLM ecosystem, providing a unified interface and management layer for interacting with language models. The rapid development pace in this space has produced powerful tools that solve real problems for organizations deploying AI systems at scale. However, speed of innovation must not come at the expense of fundamental security practices. The vulnerabilities documented here are not novel attack classes; they include missing authorization checks, path traversal, RCE via dynamic module loading, and insecure password storage. These are well-understood security issues with established mitigation patterns. Their presence in production code highlights a concerning trend: as the AI and LLM ecosystem races forward, traditional security fundamentals are sometimes treated as secondary concerns.

items.title: Cyber incident hits grocery stores in US, Netherlands and Belgium
items.summary: Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch multinational retailer, announced Monday it was taking precautionary measures following a cybersecurity incident, with stores in the U.S., Netherlands and Belgium reportedly impacted. Distribution centers, online grocery orders and in-store pricing have been disrupted, although it is unclear whether this was due to the incident itself or the precautionary measures. The company said its teams “are taking steps to assess and mitigate the issue,” including “taking some systems offline to help protect them.” Albert Heijn's website, app and customer service were unavailable, grocery deliveries were suspended, and electronic shelf labels displayed outdated promotional prices. The brand said it had disconnected systems to protect its IT environment but gave no timeline for restoring services.

items.title: U.S. Shuts Down Over 40 Laptop Farms, Charges 14 in North Korean IT Worker Fraud
items.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) on Tuesday charged 14 people and seized about 187 computers as part of its ongoing efforts to disrupt North Korea's fraudulent remote IT worker (ITW) scheme. The indictment charges a mix of U.S. citizens and Chinese nationals for their roles in an IT worker conspiracy affecting more than 70 U.S. companies, charging them with wire fraud conspiracy, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to commit identity theft, and aggravated identity theft. Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, which investigated indicators associated with suspected fake IT workers and identified links between apparently unrelated employees and laptop-hosting locations, said the threat actors have resorted to a variety of techniques to direct employer-provided hardware to laptop farm addresses during the onboarding phase. The FBI said it also identified cases where the threat actors have used threats of physical violence against former managers and their families to demand payments and coerce others to carry out actions that further the scheme, marking a newfound escalation of the threat. Besides using stolen identities to apply for jobs, the IT workers are known to falsely claim ownership of social media accounts, professional profiles, and online identities belonging to other individuals in the tech sector to lend a veneer of legitimacy to their applications.

items.title: AI-Found Linux Kernel Flaw Gives Local Users Root, and Can Break a Guest Out to the Host
items.summary: A flaw in Linux's vhost subsystem lets a local user read and write kernel memory at will and become root across nearly a decade of kernel versions. In one virtualization setup, it lets an untrusted virtual machine write to the host's memory and hijack the program that runs the virtual machine. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-74580 and named Vghost. Tencent Zhuque Lab, which found the flaw, released a fix on August 3 and published a full write-up on October 12 with working demos of both attacks. There is no public sign it has been exploited yet. vhost keeps a small cache of the memory mappings behind each virtual ring and the shared queues it uses to move data. A cache hit is treated as proof that the region was already checked. The cache is cleared when the mapping is updated or invalidated and when the queue is reset, but not when the VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR or VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM commands change the ring's addresses or size while the queue is live. The flaw affects Linux kernels from 4.11 up to 7.2-rc4. Tencent reproduced the full local-user-to-root chain on five distribution kernels: Ubuntu 26.04, RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Microsoft Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2. On Ubuntu, the device node was limited to the kvm group, so the starting point there was a member of that group rather than any user.

items.title: Heart Monitor Firm Notifying at Least 370,000 Patients of Hack
items.summary: The San Francisco, California-based company in recent days submitted breach reports to several state attorneys general, including Texas and South Carolina. iRhythm reported nearly 300,000 Texans and nearly 70,000 South Carolinians affected in those two states alone. But in recent days, a handful of media outlets, including BeInsure, reported that the iRhythm incident affected a total of nearly 8.2 million people. iRhythm in a June 10 filing to the SEC said it received demands from a threat actor for an undisclosed payment in exchange for not publicly releasing the stolen data, including proprietary data, patient protected health information and other personal information. Other hacks include an Iranian hacktivist attack on medical equipment maker Stryker in February that affected manufacturing and distribution processes for several weeks; a cyber incident at device maker Medtronic in April that affected corporate IT systems; and an August cyberattack on Boston Scientific that triggered a global network outage, shutting down manufacturing plants and distribution centers.

items.title: Global takedown hits network behind 1 billion phishing messages
items.summary: A massive cybercriminal ecosystem facilitating more than a billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations across 150 countries has been disrupted by law enforcement agencies and partners worldwide. Since the start of the year, more than 750 million malicious messages have been aimed at Microsoft customers via email and SMS texts. Following an investigation initiated by Microsoft and Japan’s National Police Agency (NPA) into a wave of fraudulent activity, "a sprawling Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace" was discovered, with tools and services for phishing campaigns. Under an order from the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, Microsoft and Health-ISAC seized and redirected domains supporting YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man. The tech giant also deactivated over 20,000 accounts associated with the YAM Store and blocked 100,000 domains the cybercriminals used for impersonation and fraud. Currently, more infrastructure is being removed based on the findings of the investigation, which also involves the Japanese authorities, JC3, Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint, and TRM Labs.

items.summary: Classification: Critical, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Functional, CVSSv3.1: 9.8, CVEs: CVE-2026-76519, Summary: A vulnerability in the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature of Cisco Secure Email Gateway could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to write arbitrary files on the underlying operating system. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending an email that contains a crafted attachment through an affected device. items.title: curl Patches HTTP/2 Upload Flaw After PoC Demonstrates Client-Side Code Execution
items.summary: A flaw in how curl handles HTTP/2 uploads lets a malicious server receiving an upload corrupt the client's memory, and the researcher who reported it turned that into code execution on the uploading machine. The curl project fixed it on October 14 in curl 8.23.0. Taking over a client needs exact knowledge of its build and memory layout, and curl expects a real attack to end in a crash instead. The flaw, a use-after-free tracked as CVE-2026-92392, affects curl and libcurl 8.12.0 through 8.22.0, both the command-line tool and the library that many other programs use for transfers. curl rates it High on its own four-level scale, its first High-severity flaw since the SOCKS5 heap overflow of October 2023. The project cut its release cycle by two weeks to ship the fix.

items.title: Cisco patches new Secure Email Gateway zero-day exploited in attacks
items.summary: Cisco has patched another actively exploited zero-day flaw in its Secure Email Gateway (SEG) that lets remote unauthenticated attackers execute commands with root privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-76519, this vulnerability stems from a relative path traversal weakness in SEG's Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature, caused by improper handling of email attachments. Threat actors can exploit this issue by sending an email with a maliciously crafted attachment through an unpatched device. "A successful exploit could allow the attacker to write arbitrary files and execute commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system," Cisco said in a Wednesday advisory. "In October 2026, the Cisco PSIRT became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability."

items.title: CISA warns admins to immediately fix Ivanti flaw exploited as zero-day
items.summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) urged security teams to immediately patch an Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) flaw exploited in zero-day attacks since at least October 1st. Tracked as CVE-2026-104935, this high-severity authentication bypass vulnerability lets remote threat actors without privileges execute arbitrary commands on targeted ICS systems in low-complexity attacks that don't require user interaction. Ivanti released ICS versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.3.0, 25.1.3.1, and 25.1.1.2 on Tuesday to address this security flaw and warned customers to "act immediately" because of "limited exploitation in the wild."

items.title: Ransomware gets personal: 'We-know-where-you-are kind of stuff'
items.summary: Tim Beasley, a senior incident response consultant at Semperis, was investigating a cyberattack involving Russia’s Midnight Blizzard when a package containing nesting dolls and other regional gifts showed up on his doorstep. At the time, Beasley served as the lead investigator for Microsoft’s Detection and Response Team (DART). He assumed it was from the group, which has been linked to the Kremlin’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), although the sender didn’t leave a note. “Just little souvenirs and gift basket stuff from that area of the world,” he told The Register. “We-know-where-you-are kind of stuff. It’s a real eye-opener when you get that type of thing.” This type of psychological intimidation and harm against victim companies’ employees has seen an uptick in the last several years to the point where it's almost common. Thirty-seven percent of ransomware attacks involved psychological or physical threats against staff, according to Semperis’ annual ransomware risk report. The global study of 1,200 post-ransomware organizations conducted over the first half of the year found attackers threatening psychological intimidation (23 percent) and physical threats (17 percent), to force payment. They are not only targeting executives and staff, but also families of their victims. The takeaway for defenders and executives from this report is to “stand your ground,” Beasley said. “Don’t buckle under the pressure, and just know that you know it's going to be okay. If you feel like you're under duress, then by all means get law enforcement involved. Don't be afraid to call the cops. Don't be afraid to get the FBI involved, sooner rather than later. And don’t pay them.”

At the time, Beasley served as the lead investigator for Microsoft’s Detection and Response Team (DART). He assumed it was from the group, which has been linked to the Kremlin’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), although the sender didn’t leave a note.

“Just little souvenirs and gift basket stuff from that area of the world,” he told The Register. “We-know-where-you-are kind of stuff. It’s a real eye-opener when you get that type of thing.”

This type of psychological intimidation and harm against victim companies’ employees has seen an uptick in the last several years to the point where it's almost common. Thirty-seven percent of ransomware attacks involved psychological or physical threats against staff, according to Semperis’ annual ransomware risk report. 

The global study of 1,200 post-ransomware organizations conducted over the first half of the year found attackers threatening psychological intimidation (23 percent) and physical threats (17 percent), to force payment. They are not only targeting executives and staff, but also families of their victims. 

The takeaway for defenders and executives from this report is to “stand your ground,” Beasley said. “Don’t buckle under the pressure, and just know that you know it's going to be okay. If you feel like you're under duress, then by all means get law enforcement involved. Don't be afraid to call the cops. Don't be afraid to get the FBI involved, sooner rather than later. And don’t pay them.”

items.title: Break the silence: Kazakhstan-nexus UAT-6275 targets CIS government organizations
items.summary: Cisco Talos identified UAT-6275 (TAG-193 by Recorded Future) activity targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Recovered artifacts show additional interest in water resources and energy. This focus is consistent with intelligence collection and may reflect the regional effects of the Russia–Ukraine war. - In activity observed from June 2025 through August 2026, Talos identified four infection-chain types that use macro-enabled documents, PS2EXE downloaders, GitHub-hosted PowerShell, and a crafted WinRAR archive exploiting CVE-2025-8088. The recovered payloads include several custom reverse shells that provide interactive remote access. - Three publicly accessible staging directories and GitHub repository history exposed payload builds, tool inventories, and changes to command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. These operational security lapses gave us direct visibility into the group's recent activity. - The files recovered from the exposed infrastructure suggest preparation for post-compromise operations and potential activity against Linux hosts and internet-facing appliances.
